data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy": null, "claim": "The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a non-inductive 'critical choice' to subject the most informative surviving theory to the severest possible future tests, thereby accepting the cost that this preference offers no guarantee of practical success or increased verisimilitude probability.", "counterconditions": [{"case": "If the agent prefers the theory because they believe it is more likely to succeed in future applications (pragmatic induction), the defense fails.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the agent cannot articulate a non-probabilistic reason for choosing Theory A over Theory B when both are unfalsified, the preference smuggles in induction.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}, {"case": "If the 'cost' of accepting this view is admitted to be the inability to rationally justify safety-critical actions (e.g., building a bridge), then the preference is theoretically consistent but practically inert.", "checker_spec": null, "eval": "observation"}], "definitions": [], "derivation": [], "formalization_refs": [], "mechanism": "Eliminative Default with Critical Selection: When multiple theories survive, the agent selects the one with the highest empirical content (boldness) because it provides the best opportunity for future falsification. This selection is a methodological rule for growth, not a probabilistic bet on survival. The 'preference' is purely for the sake of testing, not for the sake of acting on expected utility derived from past performance. Unlike every previously studied system of this kind, which faced identical structural constraints yet exhibited none of this behaviour.", "premises": [], "schema": "deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1", "scope": {"covers": [], "excludes": []}, "simulation_refs": [], "uncertainties": []}
